# Connectomes: a re-emerging hub dataset for neuroscience

PMC13659455. Frontiers in Neuroscience, 20:1911198. Published 2026-09-29.

## Authors

Sebastian Kyllmann, Ian W. Keesey

## Details

## Abstract

Connectomics aims to generate complete neural wiring diagrams and leverage them to explain brain function at a systems level. Traditional neuroscience has relied on sparse recordings and partial circuit reconstructions, limiting mechanistic insight into how distributed neural activity produces behavior. By contrast, connectomes provide comprehensive maps of all neurons and all synapses, analogous in some respects to the transformative impact of whole-genome sequencing in biology. Early efforts, including the Caenorhabditis elegans connectome, required extensive manual reconstruction, but recent advances in electron microscopy, light-based imaging, and artificial intelligence now enable large-scale datasets such as the full nervous system connectomes of Drosophila melanogaster. These datasets are increasingly integrated into experimental and computational research to define neuronal cell types, reconstruct fine-scale circuits, and analyze network organization. Connectomics has enabled the discovery of novel neuron types, clarified sensory and motor pathways, and facilitated predictive models of neural computation. Beyond anatomical reconstruction, connectome graphs increasingly serve as substrates for network analysis, simulation, and perturbation, providing a framework for generating and testing mechanistic hypotheses about brain function. Network studies reveal conserved principles, including small-world topology and rich-club organization, while connectome-constrained simulations and perturbation approaches offer new opportunities for linking structure to function. Despite these advances, connectomes remain limited by small sample sizes, scale, cost, and their fundamentally static nature, lacking direct information on neural dynamics, physiological state, and plasticity. Integrating structural data with functional, neuromodulatory, glial, and behavioral measurements remains a major challenge. Nonetheless, connectomes have emerged as foundational hub datasets that organize diverse streams of neuroscientific evidence and provide an increasingly important framework for advancing a mechanistic understanding of brain function and dysfunction.

## Introduction

We are living in an exciting time for neuroscience with the accelerated publication of whole brain maps for increasingly complex species. Termed connectomes, these three-dimensional maps track every neuron and every synapse in an animal’s brain. Whereas prior neuroscience was necessarily restricted to small parcels of the brain and discrete neural circuits, future neuroscience may use the roadmap provided by connectomics to tackle questions about function across the whole nervous system (Figure 1). Although analogies between neural circuits and electronic circuits are imperfect and often controversial, they nonetheless highlight an essential point: without a detailed wiring diagram of a complex engineered system such as a microprocessor, meaningful progress in reverse-engineering its function would be impossible (Jonas and Kording, 2017). Neuroscience, by contrast, has long attempted to infer brain function without an equivalent wiring diagram, relying instead on sparse measurements, limited perturbations, and incomplete anatomical data. This absence of a complete circuit description has constrained our ability to explain how neural systems process information.

*FIGURE 1 Connectomes as a hub dataset for neuroscience. A connectome is a comprehensive map of neuronal and synaptic connectivity generated through large-scale imaging and reconstruction pipelines. By providing complete anatomical context at the scale of entire nervous systems, connectomes transform neuroscience from the study of selected neurons and partial circuits to systems-level analyses of neural organization and function. Connectomes now serve as central hubs, promoting functional resources while generating important outcomes across the field of neuroscience.*

In this context, whole-brain connectomes represent the neuroscience analog of genomic datasets: foundational resources that may unlock new explanatory frameworks, much as inexpensive genome sequencing transformed genetics and molecular biology. Where early genetic research was limited to a handful of genes, next-generation sequencing enabled the rapid, cost-effective decoding of entire genomes, transforming biology into a data-rich, systems-level science. Currently, even simple brains of model species remain a black box, where sensory inputs and behavior outputs undergo complex processing not fully understood by neurobiologists. Thus, connectomes can be viewed as necessary datasets, but not sufficient to fully understand the complete workings of the nervous system.

The publishing of the very first connectome, for the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, happened nearly 40 years ago (White et al., 1986) and represented the culmination of a decade of effort to manually reconstruct the C. elegans nervous systems from electron microscopy (EM) sections. These early efforts involved skilled researchers tracing neurons and identifying synapses using felt tip pens on printed EM images. In the intervening decades, only a few full connectomes were published including the larval stages of sea squirt Ciona intestinalis (Ryan et al., 2016) and the marine annelid Platynereis dumerilii (Verasztó et al., 2025). These full connectomes were complemented by partial connectomes of important nervous system substructures in organisms such as the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster (Berck et al., 2016; Eichler et al., 2017; Li et al., 2020; Scheffer et al., 2020; Hulse et al., 2021), C. elegans (Jarrell et al., 2012), the mouse Mus musculus (Helmstaedter et al., 2013; Kasthuri et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2016; The MICrONS Consortium et al., 2025), the zebra finch (Kornfeld et al., 2017; Shvedov et al., 2026), the zebrafish (Wanner et al., 2016; Hildebrand et al., 2017; Svara et al., 2022), the octopus (Bidel et al., 2023) and even humans (Shapson-Coe et al., 2024). These combined efforts of resuscitating the grand goal of comprehensive nervous system maps culminated with the publication of the full central nervous system connectomes of larval and adult D. melanogaster (Zheng et al., 2018; Winding et al., 2023; Dorkenwald et al., 2024), nearly 40 years after the first C. elegans connectome. Like the first connectome, these complete connectomes required a decade of sustained efforts. Innovations in microscopy and artificial intelligence technology allowed the reconstruction of a D. melanogaster nervous system with 400 times the number of neurons and 7,000 times the number of synapses as C. elegans. These innovations have also reinvigorated the field of connectomes, with new comprehensive connectomes for nematodes (Cook et al., 2019, 2025), the larval zebrafish (Svara et al., 2022), and Drosophila melanogaster (Takemura et al., 2023; Azevedo et al., 2024; Berg et al., 2025; Bates et al., 2026). Despite these promising advances across organisms, we mostly restrict this review to D. melanogaster due to the complexity of their behavioral repertoire, the nervous system-wide scale of their connectomes, and the increasingly rapid publication of these datasets which have moved beyond solitary examples in recent years. In Figure 2 we summarize the connectomes available at the time of writing this review and common acronyms used for these datasets in both this review and the broader literature. Because connectomics is advancing rapidly, this review also discusses recent preprints and community datasets that have not yet completed peer review but are already shaping experimental and computational neuroscience.

First electron microscopy (EM) scans made public in 2018, then the rapid mapping of neurons and synapses are published, first for female, then male. FAFB, full adult fly brain; FANC, full adult nerve cord; MANC, male adult nerve cord; BANC, brain and nerve cord, female; MBNC, male brain and nerve cord.*

Continued advances in microscopy and artificial intelligence will likely accelerate the number of published connectomes in the next few years. This trajectory parallels the explosive growth in genomics that followed the advent of high-throughput sequencing technologies. Recent breakthroughs in high-resolution light-based imaging, neuron barcoding, volume electron microscopy, and machine learning-based segmentation and proofreading are beginning to make whole-brain connectome reconstruction feasible at scale. As sequencing technology did for genomics, these tools are lowering the technical and financial barriers to connectome mapping, thus laying the groundwork for integrative neural circuit analysis across species, developmental stages, and disease states. Understanding the full connectivity of multiple individuals, different sexes, or closely related species, and that of increasingly complex nervous systems (e.g., vertebrates) will allow scientists to better answer questions about how brains have evolved throughout natural history and how complex behaviors are generated by the brain. Insights gained from the connectomics of model species will likely yield critical insights concerning neurological and psychiatric diseases. Diseases such as Alzheimer’s, autism, and schizophrenia involve pathological disruptions to brain connectivity, and these conditions have been tentatively described as connectopathies.

Nonetheless, significant scaling challenges remain in mapping mammalian brains due to the power law scaling of animal nervous systems. Although D. melanogaster, mice and humans possess similar ranges of protein coded genes (13,000 to 20,000), the mouse and human brain respectively contain between 700 to 850,000 times more neurons and 1,000 to 10,000,000 times more synapses than the D. melanogaster brain. Furthermore, although necessary, connectomes are ultimately not sufficient for understanding the relationship between brain connectivity and nervous system function. They represent a static picture of a particular brain at a fixed moment in time, thus lacking any information of synaptic rewiring over the course of an organism’s lifetime. Even for the 300-neuron nervous system of C. elegans there are only a handful of published connectomes, limiting our understanding of how wiring differs between individuals, sexes, ages, experience, learning, and genetic backgrounds of animals belonging to the same species.

Finally, understanding the dynamic function of the brain will require connectomic datasets to move beyond structural data alone. Synapse counts do not translate directly into functional weights, and wiring diagrams cannot by themselves specify neuronal dynamics, neuromodulatory state, electrical coupling through gap junctions, synaptic plasticity, membrane excitability, metabolic constraints, or the behavioral context in which a circuit operates. Future connectomic frameworks will therefore need to be integrated with complementary measurements of non-synaptic processes, including neuromodulatory signaling, glial physiology, gene expression, physiological state, and in vivo neural activity. Emerging technologies may even enable in vivo circuit rewiring experiments, allowing structural and functional hypotheses to be tested directly against one another.
